title: Where's the shop?
goal: Asking where places are and pointing them out, using prepositions of place, and saying where you live.
bekal: ask *Cá bhfuil …?* and understand that *cá* brings urú
use *i, ar, ag, in aice le, os comhair* to say where things are
say where you live with *Tá mé i mo chónaí i …*

dialogs.title: Comhrá — Ag siúl sa chathair

notes: **Cá bhfuil — a question word that brings urú.** *Cá* means "where", and it's always followed by the form *bhfuil*, not *tá*. It's exactly the form that appears after *an* in ordinary questions. The short rule: as soon as *an* or *cá* comes first, *tá* becomes *bhfuil*.

**Ar an tsráid, leis an mbanc — preposition + an brings a change.** When the article *an* follows a preposition like *ar*, *ag*, *le*, *ó*, the noun gets urú: *ar an mbord*, *leis an mbanc*, *faoin gcathaoir*. The exception is words beginning with *s*: they get a *t* in front, *an tsráid*, and that *tsr-* is pronounced "tr". In Ulster séimhiú is used instead of urú (*ar an bhord*) — both are correct.

**Tá mé i mo chónaí — "I am in my dwelling".** Irish has no single verb for "to live, to reside". Instead it uses *i* + possessive + *cónaí*: *i mo chónaí* (I), *i do chónaí* (you), *ina chónaí* (he), *ina cónaí* (she). The possessive is what changes, not the verb.

**Os comhair na heaglaise — the second word changes form.** After compound prepositions like *os comhair* (in front of), *in aice* (near), *i lár* (in the middle of), the next noun goes into the possessive form: *eaglais* → *na heaglaise*, *cathair* → *na cathrach*. This form is called the genitive and is covered fully at A2; for now, just learn each pair as a unit.

blocks.text: One pattern for everything: *Cá bhfuil* + thing. The answer is *Tá sé/sí* + place.
For direction rather than location, you also use *cá*, but with a different verb: *Cá bhfuil tú ag dul?* — "where are you going?" The answer uses *go*: *Tá mé ag dul go Gaillimh*.
These ten prepositions cover nearly everything you need day to day. Watch the last column: some of them change the first letter of the next word.

blocks.title: Sa — the most common preposition, and the trickiest
items: *Sa* is *i* + *an* fused, so it means "in the". *Sa siopa* = in the shop. *Sa bhaile* = at home.
*Sa* brings **séimhiú**, not urú: *sa charr*, *sa bhaile*, *sa chistin*. But it doesn't touch *d, t, s*: *sa doras*, *sa teach*, *sa siopa*.
Before a vowel it becomes *san*: *san oifig*, *san uisce*. And for plurals it's *sna*: *sna siopaí* (in the shops).
*Sa bhaile* means "at home", while *abhaile* means "home(wards)". Two words that sound almost the same but point in opposite directions.

blocks.text: Irish splits "here" and "there" into three distances, much like the old English here–there–yonder.
They're often combined for precision: *thall ansin* ("over there"), *thíos ansiúd* ("down yonder"), *istigh anseo* ("in here"). These combinations sound very natural and are worth copying.

blocks.title: Don't mix them up: seo/sin attach, anseo/ansin stand alone
items: *Seo* and *sin* describe a thing and come **after** the noun: *an teach seo* (this house), *an fear sin* (that man).
*Anseo* and *ansin* describe a place and stand on their own: *Tá mé anseo* (I'm here), *Tá sé ansin* (it's there).
To point while introducing, use *Seo é* (here he/it is) and *Seo í* (here she is): *Seo é Seán*, *Seo í Máire*.

items: You point at the chair beside you: Tá an chathaoir ____ .
You point at a shop near the person you're talking to: Tá an siopa ____ .

Máire is inside the house: Tá Máire ____ .
You say that you yourself are here: Tá mé ____ .
